title: Code Quality — ESLint, Prettier, and TypeScript Strict Mode

subChunks.title: Code Quality — ESLint, Prettier, and TypeScript Strict Mode
subChunks.hookHtml: Code quality tools are not about style preferences — they're about catching bugs before runtime. ESLint with React-specific rules prevents common mistakes like missing dependency arrays and invalid hook calls. TypeScript's strict mode makes the type system catch null dereferences and unchecked array accesses at compile time. Prettier eliminates formatting debates so code reviews focus on logic. Together, they form a mechanical safety net that runs on every save and every push.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
ESLint configuration (flat config)

// eslint.config.js (ESLint 9+ flat config):
import js from '@eslint/js';
import tsPlugin from '@typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin';
import tsParser from '@typescript-eslint/parser';
import reactHooks from 'eslint-plugin-react-hooks';
import reactRefresh from 'eslint-plugin-react-refresh';
import jsxA11y from 'eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y';

export default [
  js.configs.recommended,
  {
    files: ['**/*.{ts,tsx}'],
    languageOptions: { parser: tsParser },
    plugins: {
      '@typescript-eslint': tsPlugin,
      'react-hooks': reactHooks,
      'react-refresh': reactRefresh,
      'jsx-a11y': jsxA11y,
    },
    rules: {
      // TypeScript:
      '@typescript-eslint/no-explicit-any': 'error',
      '@typescript-eslint/no-unused-vars': ['error', { argsIgnorePattern: '^_' }],
      '@typescript-eslint/explicit-function-return-type': 'off', // Too verbose for React
      '@typescript-eslint/no-non-null-assertion': 'error',  // Force proper null handling

      // React Hooks:
      'react-hooks/rules-of-hooks': 'error',
      'react-hooks/exhaustive-deps': 'warn', // Warn on missing deps

      // Accessibility:
      'jsx-a11y/alt-text': 'error',
      'jsx-a11y/anchor-is-valid': 'error',

      // React Refresh (HMR):
      'react-refresh/only-export-components': 'warn',
    },
  },
];

Prettier configuration

// .prettierrc.json:
{
  "semi": true,
  "singleQuote": true,
  "trailingComma": "es5",
  "printWidth": 100,
  "tabWidth": 2,
  "arrowParens": "avoid",
  "bracketSpacing": true
}

// .prettierignore:
dist/
node_modules/
*.gen.ts          // Generated files

// package.json scripts:
"format": "prettier --write .",
"format:check": "prettier --check ."  // In CI — fails if unformatted

TypeScript strict mode

// tsconfig.json — strict mode catches real bugs:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,              // Enables all strict checks below
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,  // array[0] is T | undefined
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature": true
  }
}

// What strict mode catches:

// strictNullChecks — caught at compile time:
const user = users.find(u => u.id === id);
user.name;       // ❌ Error: user could be undefined
user?.name;      // ✅ Optional chaining

// noUncheckedIndexedAccess:
const items: string[] = ['a', 'b'];
const first = items[0];  // Type: string | undefined (not string)
if (first) first.toUpperCase(); // Must check!

// discriminated union exhaustiveness:
function processEvent(event: QuestEvent) {
  switch (event.type) {
    case 'ACCEPTED': return handleAccepted(event);
    case 'COMPLETED': return handleCompleted(event);
    // TypeScript warns if you add a new QuestEvent type without handling it here
    default: event satisfies never; // Compile error if not exhaustive
  }
}

Pre-commit hooks with lint-staged

// package.json:
"lint-staged": {
  "*.{ts,tsx}": [
    "eslint --fix",
    "prettier --write"
  ],
  "*.{js,json,css,md}": [
    "prettier --write"
  ]
}

// .husky/pre-commit:
#!/bin/sh
npx lint-staged

# Prevents committing code that fails linting
# Automatically fixes what can be auto-fixed
# Runs only on staged files — fast even in large repos

Type-safe environment variables

// env.ts — validate and type env vars at startup:
import { z } from 'zod';

const envSchema = z.object({
  VITE_API_URL: z.string().url(),
  VITE_FEATURE_FLAGS: z.string().optional(),
});

const parsed = envSchema.safeParse(import.meta.env);
if (!parsed.success) {
  console.error('Invalid environment variables:', parsed.error.format());
  throw new Error('Missing required environment variables');
}

export const env = parsed.data; // Fully typed, validated at startup

Vex: "The goal of code quality tooling is not consistency — it's bug prevention. ESLint's react-hooks/exhaustive-deps catches infinite render loops before they hit production. TypeScript's strictNullChecks catches null dereferences. noUncheckedIndexedAccess catches out-of-bounds errors. These aren't style rules; they're runtime errors caught at compile time."

storyBeats.text: A pull request adds a useEffect with a missing dependency. ESLint flags it. The developer ignores the warning and merges. Three days later, a production bug: stale closure, wrong questId, wrong data updated. The warning was the bug.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: react-hooks/exhaustive-deps is not a style rule. It's telling you about a stale closure — a function that captured an old value of a variable that's now different. Every suppressed ESLint warning is a deferred bug. If the rule is wrong, the code is wrong — fix the code, don't suppress the rule.

storyBeats.speaker: TypeScript strict mode catches real bugs

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Set up a production-grade code quality configuration:

  • Write an ESLint flat config with: TypeScript parser, react-hooks rules (rules-of-hooks as error, exhaustive-deps as warn), no-explicit-any as error, and jsx-a11y alt-text as error
  • Write a tsconfig.json with strict: true and noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true, then fix the TypeScript errors that result
  • Write a lint-staged configuration that runs eslint --fix and prettier --write on staged .ts/.tsx files
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Establish code quality standards for the quest board: (1) ESLint flat config with all recommended rules: TypeScript strict, react-hooks, jsx-a11y, and no-explicit-any. Fix all existing ESLint errors in the codebase. (2) Enable TypeScript strict mode and noUncheckedIndexedAccess — fix all resulting type errors (document any that you intentionally disable with // @ts-expect-error and a comment explaining why). (3) Configure lint-staged with Husky pre-commit hooks — verify it blocks a commit that has an unused variable. (4) Add a type-safe environment variable validation using Zod that runs at app startup and throws a descriptive error if required variables are missing.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what TypeScript's strict mode actually enables — list at least three specific checks it adds and give a concrete example of a runtime bug each one prevents. Explain the difference between ESLint rules that are 'error' vs 'warn' — when should each be used? Walk through the react-hooks/exhaustive-deps rule — what is a stale closure, why is it a bug, and how does the ESLint rule catch it?

questions.prompt: TypeScript's `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is enabled. `const items: string[] = getItems(); const first = items[0]; first.toUpperCase()` fails with a type error. Why?
options: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, array index access returns T | undefined — items[0] is string | undefined because the array might be empty. You must check for undefined before calling string methods.
getItems() returns a readonly array, which doesn't support index access
TypeScript strict mode disables array index access entirely
toUpperCase() is not a method on string in strict TypeScript
questions.answer: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess, array index access returns T | undefined — items[0] is string | undefined because the array might be empty. You must check for undefined before calling string methods.
questions.explanation: Without this flag, TypeScript assumes items[0] is always a string — but arrays can be empty. noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes TypeScript reflect reality: the item might not exist. The fix: const first = items[0]; if (first) first.toUpperCase() — or: items[0]?.toUpperCase(). This flag catches a whole class of runtime 'Cannot read properties of undefined' errors at compile time.

questions.prompt: A developer adds `// eslint-disable-next-line react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` to suppress a missing dependency warning in useEffect. When is this acceptable?
options: When the dependency is a function defined outside the component that is guaranteed to be stable (e.g., a singleton service) and adding it to deps would cause an infinite loop — document why with a comment
Whenever the developer is confident the missing dep won't cause a bug
When the component has more than 5 dependencies — the rule is impractical for complex components
Never — always add all missing dependencies; the rule is always right
questions.answer: When the dependency is a function defined outside the component that is guaranteed to be stable (e.g., a singleton service) and adding it to deps would cause an infinite loop — document why with a comment
questions.explanation: Suppressing exhaustive-deps is occasionally correct but should be rare and documented. Valid cases: a function reference that is stable by construction (module-level, outside React's rendering), a ref.current access (refs are intentionally not reactive). Invalid cases: 'it works fine without it', missing a useCallback on a function prop, or not understanding the stale closure. Always write a comment explaining the suppression: // stable singleton, never changes.
